message.content:
**Earliest non‑Christian historical reference to Jesus Christ** | Source | Date (approx.) | Passage & Context | |--------|----------------|-------------------| | **Flavius Josephus – *Antiquities of the Jews* (Book 18, Chapter 3)** | 93–94 CE | Josephus, a first‑century Jewish historian, writes:
“Now there was about this time a wise man, Jesus, a doer of wonderful works… He was crucified by Pontius Pilate at the suggestion of the chief priests.”
He also mentions “James, the brother of Jesus who was called Christ.” This is the earliest surviving mention of Jesus in a secular, non‑Christian text. | | **Tacitus – *Annals* (Book 15, Chapter 44)** | 116 CE | The Roman historian records:
“Christus, the founder of the name, was executed by Pontius Pilate during the reign of Tiberius.”
Tacitus’ account confirms the crucifixion and the existence of a movement named after Jesus. | **Christian literary sources (for comparison)** | Source | Date (approx.) | Notes | |--------|----------------|-------| | **Gospel of Mark** | 65–70 CE | Widely regarded as the earliest of the canonical Gospels; it contains the first Christian narrative of Jesus’ life. | | **Gospel of Matthew & Luke** | 80–90 CE | These later Gospels build on Mark’s account. | | **Gospel of John** | 90–110 CE | Theologically distinct, written later. | --- ### Summary - **Josephus** provides the earliest extant secular reference to Jesus, dated to the 90s CE. - **Tacitus** offers a later but independent Roman confirmation, dated to the 110s CE. - The earliest Christian narrative appears in the Gospel of Mark, written roughly 30–35 years after Jesus’ death. These references are the foundation for historians who treat Jesus as a historical figure rather than solely a theological one.
